blocks.text: The chapter’s closing vision brings together a new heaven and earth, the descent of New Jerusalem, God dwelling with humanity, and the end of death, mourning, crying, and pain. Its final city scene also includes nations walking in its light and rulers bringing their glory into it, widening the picture beyond a private or isolated hope.

Verses 3 and 22 use sanctuary language in a striking way: God dwells with humanity, yet the city has no separate temple because the Lord God and the Lamb are its temple. Sanctuary language occurs in several distinct settings—such as tabernacle, temples, Christological metaphor, community metaphor, heavenly sanctuary, and new creation—so this vision should not simply be collapsed into any one earlier referent. Its emphasis here is direct divine presence and holiness within the city.

The New Jerusalem gathers several images at once: city, bride, sanctuary, Eden, and renewed Zion. Revelation also repeatedly reworks imagery from Israel’s Scriptures, including Ezekielian visions of throne, measuring, city, river, and tree. This helps explain why the vision is richly layered rather than limited to a single literal image category.
